What caused the record-breaking, prolonged heatwave in northern Vietnam this autumn?
This winter will be warmer, with temperatures in Northern Vietnam 1 to 1.5 degrees Celsius higher than the multi-year average, and less severe cold spells.
The beginning of Autumn in 2026 starts on August 7th (June 25th in the lunar calendar), marking the beginning of the autumn season according to the 24 solar terms. Many people believe that after the beginning of Autumn, the weather usually becomes cooler, with less intense heat. However, in the very first days of Autumn this year, Northern and Central Vietnam experienced a widespread heatwave, with some areas experiencing intense heat, making the weather hot, humid, and stifling.
Although it's already the beginning of October, the middle of autumn in Northern Vietnam, the weather in recent days has remained quite hot, especially in Hanoi and the Northern Delta region. Some areas in the North have experienced temperatures of 35-37 degrees Celsius, which is quite high compared to the usual perception of autumn weather.
According to statistics, from September to the present, the North has recorded 55 record-breaking temperatures; for example, at Yen Chau station (Son La) and Muong Te station ( Lai Chau ), intense heat ranging from 38 to 38.3 degrees Celsius still occurred in early October, exceeding the previous record by nearly 1 degree Celsius.
The average temperature across the region is significantly higher than in previous years due to the infrequent and weak occurrence of cold air masses, with the two cold fronts on September 10th and October 4th only causing a slight drop in temperature.
Explaining this unusual weather phenomenon, Mr. Nguyen Van Huong, representative of the National Center for Meteorological and Hydrological Forecasting, said that the main cause is the influence of the El Nino phenomenon, which creates a stable air mass covering the Northern region, resulting in more sunshine and preventing cold air from moving southward.
Currently, sea surface temperatures in the Nino 3.4 region have risen to 2.4 degrees Celsius, indicating that El Nino is approaching its strongest intensity since 1950 and is forecast to last until March next year, causing temperatures in Northern Vietnam to remain higher than normal.

According to Mr. Nguyen Van Huong, this winter will be warmer, with temperatures in the North higher than the multi-year average by 1 to 1.5 degrees Celsius, and severe cold spells will occur later and less frequently. However, a warm winter does not mean that severe cold spells will not occur, so localities and people, especially in high mountainous areas, need to closely monitor the forecast to proactively protect their health, crops, and livestock.
Forecasts indicate a moderate-intensity cold front will arrive around the beginning of next week, bringing rain and bringing temperatures down to cool levels in the North. Severe cold spells and frost are likely to occur in late December and early January.
Responding to the impacts of El Nino
Dr. Truong Ba Kien, Deputy Executive Director of the Center for Meteorological and Climate Research, Institute of Meteorology, Hydrology, Environment and Marine Sciences , said that strong to very strong El Nino events often increase the likelihood of high temperatures, prolonged heatwaves, lack of rain, drought, water shortages, and saltwater intrusion.
However, the impacts are not uniform across all regions and do not necessarily occur precisely when El Nino peaks. In Vietnam, some significant effects may be more apparent during the dry season and the hot months of early 2027.
In the North, the most prominent impact of El Nino is a tendency for temperatures to be higher than average, especially during winter. The number of severe cold spells may decrease, winters will be warmer, and the duration of cold spells will be shorter. Strong cold fronts may still occur from time to time, depending on the development of cold air masses and other weather patterns.
During the hot season, the North continues to experience intense heat waves. A prolonged lack of rainfall could also lead to drought and localized water shortages in some areas, especially those heavily reliant on surface water sources.
Meanwhile, the Central and Central Highlands regions need to pay more attention to water resources for production and daily life. The South Central coastal region has many arid areas, short river systems, and water resources heavily dependent on rainfall. The Central Highlands, on the other hand, has a high demand for water for agriculture .

Dr. Truong Ba Kien stated that during prolonged dry periods, soil moisture decreases, and the amount of water flowing into rivers, streams, and reservoirs can be low, putting pressure on crops, production, and livelihoods. Prolonged dry and hot conditions also increase the risk of forest fires.
Nationwide, El Nino also alters some characteristics of the typhoon season. The number of typhoons and tropical depressions in the South China Sea tends to be lower than average, but storms with unusual trajectories or intensity can still occur. Localized heavy rainfall, thunderstorms, tornadoes, lightning, flash floods, and landslides also need to be monitored throughout the season.
According to Dr. Truong Ba Kien, the significant impact of El Nino may not appear immediately when the phenomenon peaks at the end of 2026, but will be more apparent during the dry and hot season of early 2027. This is also the period when people need to proactively adjust their lives to adapt to high temperatures, prolonged droughts, and potentially increased water and electricity consumption.
For the central provinces, the Central Highlands, and the Mekong Delta, proactively managing water resources is even more crucial. People can conserve water in daily life and production, inspect water storage and distribution systems, and monitor water levels in reservoirs, rivers, and streams, as well as information on saltwater intrusion. For agricultural production, adjusting planting seasons, crop structures, or irrigation methods according to water availability can also help reduce pressure during prolonged droughts.

MANILA, Philippines – The education sector will not be spared when El Niño worsens in the coming months. Across the country, temperatures are expected to be warmer than usual, which would pose another threat to students’ learning.
Education Secretary Sonny Angara previously said government protocols would ensure that El Niño’s effects are mitigated in public schools.
How exactly is the Department of Education (DepEd) preparing for the impact of the weather phenomenon? Pending formal guidelines, here’s what we know so far:
How to conduct classes
In an interview with Rappler on Friday, October 23, Education Undersecretary Malcolm Garma said the DepEd is concerned that lost school days may increase due to high heat index levels. The heat index, or the temperature that the human body perceives, is measured using the air temperature and the relative humidity in a place at a given time.
Garma noted that the DepEd’s existing class suspension guidelines, issued back in June, already spell out learning continuity plans for schools.
The DepEd said that under Level 1-Hayo, face-to-face classes continue during manageable conditions. Schools can set scheduled water breaks, shift outdoor activities to early morning or shaded areas, and allow students to wear comfortable clothing or Physical Education attire.
At Level 2-Hinay, schools may adopt modified class days with structured home-based or hybrid learning.
Level 3-Hinga may be implemented when temperatures can cause heat cramps or heat exhaustion or there is loss of water supply. Learning packets, short activities, and broadcast resources may be used to reduce academic demands.
Once the heat index reaches 42°C and above, academic activities are suspended at Level 4-Hinto, focusing on safety checks and psychosocial support referrals, according to the class suspension guidelines.
Garma said self-learning modules, activity sheets, and other materials needed for alternative learning will be prepositioned before the peak months of intense heat.
What if the heat is unbearable?
In case actual conditions turn out to be worse than projected, Garma said school heads can adjust class schedules or recommend granular suspensions of face-to-face classes. But he added that the situation must be properly assessed.
“Hindi naman ‘yung school head ay basta-basta na lang siyang magpapauwi o magsu-suspend. So kailangan mai-vet ito ng [schools] division office…or [they should] even coordinate with the local government unit. Para sa gano’n, talagang hindi naman maabuso din ‘yung pagsususpende ng klase,” the DepEd official said.
(The school head cannot just decide to send students home or suspend classes. This must be vetted by the schools division office or they should even coordinate with the local government unit. This is to prevent abuse of class suspensions.)
“While we are looking after…the welfare of our learners, we also have to ensure that learning continues. At alam naman natin na pinakamainam pa din na learning delivery natin ay kung school-based ito or face-to-face (And we know that the best learning delivery is school-based or face-to-face),” he added.
Measures for water supply, health
Garma said the DepEd has ordered schools to make hydration facilities and equipment, such as safe drinking stations and water dispensers, accessible to learners and personnel.
The DepEd also told schools to repair water leaks immediately and coordinate closely with local water concessionaires for rationing contingencies.
Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian earlier raised the possibility of deploying community water depots to public schools. These depots are rainwater catchment equipment with built-in filtration systems to provide potable water during shortages. Garma said the DepEd welcomes such proposals.
Regarding health, Garma said school clinics will be ready to address medical concerns like heat stroke or dehydration. Additional support from local government units (LGUs) and the Department of Health will also be tapped for emergency response.
With El Niño also threatening agriculture and food supply, schools division offices and schools were directed to develop contingency menus for the school-based feeding program, partner with LGUs and cooperatives for local food sourcing, and maintain buffer stocks of shelf-stable commodities.
How about school buildings?
Garma said public schools can use their funding for maintenance and other operating expenses to buy additional ventilators like electric fans.
But the DepEd’s long-term solution is structural intervention.
“For old classrooms, we cannot change their designs; we can only do mitigation. But for those classrooms under construction and for future ones, we’ll make sure that there will be structural intervention such as high ceilings, insulated ceilings, and wide airflow,” he said in Filipino.
Garma also said the DepEd is exploring the possibility of institutionalizing the use of solar power in schools to reduce electricity costs and possibly provide air-conditioning.
The DepEd said its upcoming formal guidelines for El Niño-related measures will mandate schools to conduct integrated school-level risk assessments covering water supply reliability, classroom thermal safety, electricity resilience, and fire hazard prevention.
The set of guidelines is also expected to prohibit schools from charging or requiring parents to buy cooling equipment, connectivity, or specialized attire as a condition for alternative learning modalities. – Rappler.com
